text.p: President Bill Clinton, emerging from what he has proclaimed to be a successful U.S. showdown with Iraq, hit the campaign trail on Thursday to highlight his proposals for education and health care.

The stop in Tampa was the first in a two-day swing through Florida, a populous state that has not gone Democratic in a presidential election in 20 years but where recent polls show Clinton slightly ahead of Republican challenger Bob Dole.
Clinton sounded familiar themes on education in his first speech, including hooking school rooms up to the international web of computers on the Internet and a $10,000 tax break for college tuition.

"A big part of building a bridge to the 21st century is building a bridge big enough to give every single boy and girl in America a chance to live up to their God-given abilities," he told several hundred students at Hillsborough High School.
"This is an important part of building the future we desire. I am committed to it and I want you to be committed to it," he said.

Dole needs to hang on to Florida if he is to have any chance of upsetting the Democratic president on Nov. 5. But two of his top strategists, Don Sipple and Mike Murphy, quit his faltering campaign on Thursday in what the Dole camp called a friendly departure.

"Clearly ... they are in conflict over which way to go, what message to pursue," said Clinton campaign spokesman Joe Lockhart, who was travelling with the president. "I think it was inevitable that there would be another shakeup."

Clinton, riding a strong rise in his poll ratings after last week's Democratic convention and the U.S. air strikes on Iraq, resumed campaigning after spending much of the week concentrating on the Iraqi crisis.
On Wednesday, he declared that U.S. cruise missile strikes had taught Iraqi President Saddam Hussein the desired lesson against aggressive behaviour towards Iraq's Kurdish minorities,

A Reuters poll by John Zogby Group International, released on Thursday, said Clinton got a big boost from both the Iraqi crisis and the convention publicity and regained a 15-point lead over Dole nationwide, 48-33 percent.

In returning to the stump, Clinton chose a state no Democratic presidential candidate has won since Jimmy Carter in 1976. He was to head later to Broward County near Miami to speak to senior citizens on health care and his support for a bill to bar health maintenance organisations from restricting what treatment procedures doctors may discuss with patients.
Retirees are a major component of the Florida electorate.

He was also to announce plans to name a new health care commission to study financing and changes in the industry and their impact on patients. The commission, which is to report to the president next year, is to be co-chaired by Health and Human Services Secretary Donna Shalala and Labour Secretary Robert Reich, White House spokeswoman Mary Ellen Glynn said.
It will deal with issues -- financing and care quality -- Clinton had hoped to address in his failed effort to pass legislation to provide health insurance for all Americans.
Later the president was to attend a Democratic fundraiser where some $600,000 was being raised to help candidates.
On Friday Clinton was to head for Orlando to address the National Baptist Convention, one of the largest black religious organisations in the world.
